Situation1: They are expected to be present at a family dinner or small gathering.
Expectation2: Challenge unfair systems and influence policy change
Situation2: They raise concerns about a policy that seems to disadvantage certain youth, seniors, or refugee applicants.
Story: I stared at my phone, the group chat with my family lighting up with reminders about tonight’s dinner. Mom’s message was clear: “It means a lot to your brother if you’re there.” I knew how much these gatherings mattered, especially after Dad’s health scare last year. But my mind kept drifting to the city council meeting scheduled for the same evening. As an advocate, I’d spent weeks preparing to speak out against a new policy that would make it harder for refugee youth to access support. My colleagues were counting on me to be the voice that challenged the system, to stand up for those who couldn’t be in the room. The weight of both roles pressed on me—my family’s need for togetherness, my responsibility to the community. I could almost hear my brother’s disappointment if I missed dinner, but I also pictured the faces of the youth who might lose their chance if I stayed silent. My heart pounded as I tried to figure out how to be both the sibling my family needed and the advocate my community depended on.
